Sometimes there is no answer key. You have hundreds of CTD profiles and no water-mass
classification, or a community matrix with two dozen taxa and no hypothesis about how they
group. Unsupervised methods look for structure in the data itself.

They are genuinely useful, and they are the easiest methods in the course to over-read.
Every one of them always returns an answer: k-means returns $k$ clusters whether or not
clusters exist, and a principal component is a direction of large variance, which is not
the same thing as an ecological gradient. Nothing in the output says "nothing found".

So this section runs the methods and then spends as long again asking whether what came
back was real.

## What this section found

- Clustering 24 taxon counts recovered the **hard-bottom / soft-bottom** split of the
  seabed with **15 stations out of 800** on the wrong side — from counts alone, having
  never seen a substrate column.
- Depth is **99.4%** of the variance of the raw environmental table. Clustering those
  columns without standardising is clustering depth, and nothing else.
- The average silhouette width of that successful clustering was **0.179**, which the
  circulating rules of thumb call "no substantial structure". Against column-shuffled data
  it is nearly **five times** the no-structure floor.
- Four criteria for the number of clusters gave **two, three, six** and no answer at all.
  `clusGap()`'s default reference chose six; a permutation reference chose two, which is
  the truth.
- One distance matrix and four linkage rules gave agreement with the true split ranging
  from **0.005** (single linkage) to **0.889** (Ward). `hclust()`'s default scored 0.332 at
  $k=2$.
- Both real gradients in the data lie at about **45°** to the principal axes — 139° and
  41° — because they carry almost the same variance and PCA has no way to choose between
  rotations.
- Rules for how many components to keep said **16**, **7** and **3**. Cross-validated
  prediction said **two**: two components predicted station depth to 21.2 m, and all 24
  did no better.
- Bootstrap stability was **bimodal** — 53 replicates found the substrate split, 7 found a
  depth split, nothing landed in between — and its mean of 0.881 described neither.

::: {.callout-important}
The most stable result in the section is the one that corresponds to nothing. Splitting
the soft-bottom stations by depth reproduces at an adjusted Rand index of 0.890 and never
drops below 0.71 — and the data contains no soft-sediment assemblages, only a continuous
turnover that k-means cut in the same place every time. **Stability is necessary and not
sufficient.** A stable algorithm cuts a stable gradient in a stable place.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Two habits run through every page here. **Put your data through a structure-free null** —
shuffle each column independently, keeping every variable's own distribution and
destroying co-occurrence — and run the identical pipeline on it, because almost no
unsupervised statistic can be read on an absolute scale. And **check the result against a
variable the method never saw**; agreement with a *categorical* one is evidence of groups,
while agreement with a *binned continuous* one is only ever evidence of a gradient.

A gradient is a finding. "Composition turns over continuously with depth" is a more honest
sentence than any cluster count, and on this data it is the true one.
:::
